content: The newton, denoted by the symbol N, is the SI-derived unit of force. It is named after Sir Isaac Newton in honor of his contributions to classical mechanics. A force of approximately 9.8 N is required to counteract the gravitational pull on a mass of 1 kilogram (such as a small apple) under standard Earth gravity. This is often approximated as 10 N for practical purposes in everyday life and engineering, serving as a convenient rule of thumb. The decanewton (daN), equivalent to 10 N, is increasingly used in applications such as specifying the load-bearing capacity of items like ropes and anti-vibration mounts. This unit is roughly equivalent to the non-SI unit of force known as the kilogram-force (kgf). The gravitational force exerted by Earth on a human being with a mass of 70 kilograms is approximately 687 N. The scalar product of force and distance is defined as energy. In SI units, when a force of 1 N is applied over a distance of 1 meter, the resulting work done is 1 N·m, which is equivalent to 1 joule, the SI unit of energy. Since a newton represents a relatively small force, it is common to express larger forces in kilonewtons (kN), where 1 kN equals 1,000 N. For example, a force of 9.8 kN corresponds to the gravitational force on a mass of 1,000 kilograms (or 1,000 kgf) under standard Earth gravity conditions.
